subtype: Approach: hiding struggles to look capable [Pitfall]
passage: Naveen, I'll tell you about my first project as lead. I'm Kashish. I was twenty-five, a young man scared of looking weak. So every Friday my report was green. Green, green, green, for a month. Meanwhile the modules from two teams refused to talk to each other, and I stayed silent, hoping to fix it myself over weekends. I never asked my manager for help, because I thought asking meant I couldn't lead. Then, five days before release, the integration test failed on every path. My manager looked at four weeks of green reports and asked how this could be. I had no answer except the truth. We shipped late, and for a long while my reports were read with a raised eyebrow.

qa.q: How long did Kashish report everything as green?
qa.a: Kashish reported green, green, green for a month.

qa.q: Why did Kashish not ask the manager for help?
qa.a: Kashish was scared of looking weak and believed asking for help meant not being able to lead.

qa.q: What could Kashish have done at the first sign of trouble, and why?
qa.a: Kashish could have told the manager about the two modules early and asked for help, because a problem shared in the first week is much cheaper to fix than one found five days before release.

qa.q: How might the manager have felt on seeing the failed test after four weeks of green reports?
qa.a: The manager was probably surprised and let down, having trusted reports that showed no trouble at all.

grounding: Illustrates a first-time lead reporting everything as fine for a month, never asking for help, so integration trouble surfaces only days before release.

passage:
Francis had led the logistics app project for a month, and every Friday his status report said green. It wasn't. The warehouse system's data kept breaking the app's inventory screen, and his two fixes had made it worse.
The office Wi-Fi was patchy that month, and the client was in another time zone, so the weekly call was at seven in the morning, when he was barely awake. Each week he told himself: one more week and I'll fix it, then I'll mention it.
His teammate Divyansh asked once, "Want me to look at the integration?" Francis said, "It's fine, nearly done." He didn't want to look like a lead who couldn't handle his first project.
Four days before release, the full test ran. The inventory screen crashed on every second order. The manager called him in. "How long has this been happening?"
"Since the second week," Francis said quietly. The release was pushed back a month.

qa.q: How long was the release pushed back?
qa.a: The release was pushed back a month.

qa.q: Why did Francis keep reporting green, and what was he feeling?
qa.a: He was afraid of looking like a lead who couldn't handle his first project, and felt anxious hoping to fix it quietly.

qa.q: What would you change first in how Francis handled the problem?
qa.a: I would report the integration problem in the second week and accept Divyansh's offer, because early help costs far less than a late surprise.

qa.q: How might Divyansh feel after the delay?
qa.a: Divyansh may feel frustrated and a bit hurt that his offer to help was turned down while the problem grew.

grounding: Shows a lead reporting green for a month while integration problems grow, never asking for help, so the trouble surfaces days before release.

subtype: Approach: hiding struggles to look capable [Pitfall]
passage:
Omkar's first project as lead was a hospital booking app for a Bengaluru clinic chain. From week two, the payment connection kept failing in testing. He told nobody.
Every Monday his manager, Madhav, asked, "Any blockers?" and every Monday Omkar said, "All good." He stayed late trying fixes alone. He thought asking for help would make everyone wonder why they'd promoted him.
His status dashboard stayed green for five weeks. Madhav was relaxed. The client was told the launch was on track.
Then, a week before release, the full test ran with real bank sandboxes. Payments failed forty percent of the time. Madhav called an emergency meeting. "Why am I finding this out now?"
Omkar looked at his laptop. "I thought I could fix it."
Madhav had to call the client that afternoon and move the launch. Walking out, he said, "I could have got you help in week two."

qa.q: How often did payments fail in the full test?
qa.a: Payments failed forty percent of the time.

qa.q: Why did Omkar hide the problem, and what was he afraid of?
qa.a: He was afraid everyone would wonder why they had promoted him, so he felt pressure to look capable and fix it alone.

qa.q: What should Omkar have done when the payment connection first failed?
qa.a: He should have told Madhav in week two, since the manager could have brought in help before the problem grew.

qa.q: How does the situation look to Madhav?
qa.a: Madhav feels blindsided and frustrated, having to move the launch with the client when he could have helped weeks earlier.

grounding: Shows a lead hiding integration problems behind a green dashboard for weeks and not asking for help, so trouble surfaces just before release.
